A cure for diabetes

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Scientists have discovered a possible cure for diabetes

Summary:
A giant leap in the treatment of diabetes may have been discovered by Harvard researchers, who used tissues from the stomach lining to help restore insulin production. They use stem cells from the stomach lining and engineer them so that they become insulin producing T-cells. Thye then grow clusters and create mini-organs. They then implant these mini-organs in various places in a body and they control insulin levels perfectly. No more diabetes.

Further information:
This is the published abstract: Abstract of Reprogrammed Stomach Tissue as a Renewable Source of Functional β Cells for Blood Glucose Regulation
The gastrointestinal (GI) epithelium is a highly regenerative tissue with the potential to provide a renewable source of insulin+ cells after undergoing cellular reprogramming. Here, we show that cells of the antral stomach have a previously unappreciated propensity for conversion into functional insulin-secreting cells. Native antral endocrine cells share a surprising degree of transcriptional similarity with pancreatic β cells, and expression of β cell reprogramming factors in vivo converts antral cells efficiently into insulin+ cells with close molecular and functional similarity to β cells. Induced GI insulin+ cells can suppress hyperglycemia in a diabetic mouse model for at least 6 months and regenerate rapidly after ablation. Reprogramming of antral stomach cells assembled into bioengineered mini-organs in vitro yielded transplantable units that also suppressed hyperglycemia in diabetic mice, highlighting the potential for development of engineered stomach tissues as a renewable source of functional β cells for glycemic control.

This is what it means:
Harvard University scientists have made major progress in dealing with a long-standing hurdle in treating diabetic patients.

People with diabetes have high blood sugar because their pancreatic beta cells (which store and release insulin) are not producing enough insulin. In type 1 diabetes (“juvenile diabetes”), the beta cells are even destroyed. In most cases, physicians treat type 1 diabetes with insulin injections, but people with complications may require pancreas implants or pancreatic islets from another person to replace those defective beta cells.

Those are limited. When effective sources of insulin-producing cells become available in the future, replacing beta cells with transplants would be preferable because that may enable blood sugar to be better controlled without the need for lifetime injections. The problem: those insulin-producing transplants tend to be destroyed by the ongoing diabetic disease process of the person (or animal) receiving the transplant.
Ideally, for a successful transplant to survive, transplanted cells or tissues need to somehow replenish or regenerate themselves.

Reprogramming stomach cells
In the new Harvard study, published online in an open access paper in Cell Stem Cell, the researchers have finally worked out a way to do that. They discovered that the lower stomach contains cells that can be reprogrammed to act as beta cells, and thus produce insulin. The stomach and intestine also naturally contain large numbers of stem cells that can multiply to continue to replenish the dying insulin-producing cells.

The report’s senior author, Qiao Zhou, PhD, associate professor at Harvard University’s Department of Stem Cell and Regenerative Biology, made the discovery after first genetically engineering mice to express three genes that can turn other cell types into insulin-producing beta-like cells. The researchers then looked for the tissue in the body that could be most easily reprogrammed to produce insulin.

“We looked all over, from the nose to the tail of the mouse,” says Zhou. “We discovered, surprisingly, that some of the cells in the pylorus region of the stomach (connecting the stomach to the small intestine) are most amenable to conversion to beta cells. This tissue appears to be the best starting material.”*
The team found that these stomach cells were naturally similar to pancreatic beta cells and could produce insulin and reverse high blood sugar in mice for up to six months.**
Creating “mini-stomachs” for humans containing insulin-producing cells for transplantation


These initial experiments involved genetic engineering. But humans cannot yet be genetically engineered, so the researchers needed to find a version of this method that works for humans.
So the researchers took samples of the stomach tissue containing stem cells from the mice and grew them into “mini-organs” — tiny ball-like mini-stomachs that contain insulin-producing cells (that function like beta cells), as well as stem cells that can multiply to replace the insulin-producing cells as they later die after transplantation.
They transplanted these mini-organs into a membrane in the mouse’s abdomen. To test their function, the researchers then destroyed the normal insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells in the mice. They confirmed that the mini-organs compensated for the resulting loss of insulin, maintaining glucose at normal levels in five of the 22 experimental animals (this was the team’s expected success rate).
What is potentially really great about this approach (once it’s developed for humans) is that a physician will be able to create a patient-specific therapy by simply doing a biopsy (snipping out tissue for analysis) from the patient, grow the cells in the lab (as with the mice), reprogram those cells to produce insulin — and then transplant these cells directly into the patient.**
“That’s what we’re working on now,” says Zhou. “We’re very excited.”
Research funding was provided by the National Institute of Health, the HSCI, the Timothy Murphy Fund, the Children’s Hospital Boston Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities Research Center, and the Harvard Digestive Diseases Center.

Press Release:


Diabetes Cure?
It’s a lifestyle disease and a global health crisis costing billions. Carte Blanche meets the Harvard researchers who have engineered stomach cells to produce insulin. Have they made a giant leap in the race to find a cure for diabetes?


Script:


V/O:
Breakthrough research at Harvard University in Boston by this man is set to change the lives of millions of diabetics worldwide.
Prof Joe Zhou:
This could be the basis for a cure for diabetes in future.
V/O:
Professor Joe Zhou is one of the world’s leading diabetes researchers.
Joe:
Diabetes is the silent disease. There are right now, believe it or not, over two hundred million people that suffer from diabetes worldwide. So that is a huge population.
V/O:
Dr Laurence Distiller, based at the Centre for Diabetes and Endocrinology, agrees that diabetes is a global crisis.
Dr Distiller:
Diabetes is basically high blood sugar. There is a worldwide pandemic of diabetes, particularly in the developing world and South Africa is part of that.
V/O:
And, uncontrolled diabetes can be fatal.
Dr Distiller
You get heart attacks, strokes but also blindness, kidney failure, amputations, nerve damage.
V/O:
All these conditions are the eventual result of abnormally high sugar levels in the blood. In healthy people a hormone called insulin produced in the pancreas maintains normal blood sugar levels. It is produced by the so-called Islets of Langerhans which are clusters of insulin secreting Beta cells.
LINK:
The body has the ability to regulate the release of insulin with extreme precision according to changes in blood sugar levels.
Joe:
So if you eat a candy, it pumps out for example a small amount of insulin to now drive down your blood sugar level to normal. Now if you eat a big pie, it pumps up a lot more insulin to now stabilize it, to a normal level. If you eat anything for a while the insulin is shut down, so you have normal sugar level in your blood. It’s a very fine balance.
V/O:
It is the insulin producing pancreatic Beta cells that are affected in the two main types of diabetes - Type 1 and Type 2.
Distiller:
Type 1 Diabetes is a condition where Beta-cells which are the cells in the pancreas that produce insulin, stop functioning. They are destroyed.
V/O:
Type 1 usually occurs in young children who have no Beta cells. But, Type 2, which manifests later in life, is triggered by poor lifestyle, bad eating habits and minimal exercise. A resistance to insulin builds over time and their Beta cells are less efficient.
Distiller
If they have got a problem with insulin secreting cells that are fragile and don’t work as well as they should. The amount insulin they can make can’t overcome the resistance to insulin and they get diabetes.
V/O:
Diabetes is thus directly linked to Beta cells that are either destroyed or functioning poorly. Type 2 diabetics have to take medication and in advanced stages also insulin injections. Type 1 diabetics have to take insulin for life.
Joe:
It is a wonderful therapy but it is not perfect and it is not as good as your own Beta cells.
LINK:
Sometimes medical specialists transplant donor Beta cells into patients.
V/O:
Either the pancreas or clusters of Beta cells are transplanted.
Joe:
Most of the recipients can maintain normal sugar levels for a few years. Some even ten years. But eventually they fail because it is not your own organ.
LINK
The immune suppressants patients have to take to stop the body from rejecting transplants, also play a role in this. The ideal is to use a patient’s own tissue and organs for transplantation.
Joe:
So that is what my laboratory and others are aiming for. To be able to create new beta cells you’re your own tissue, from your own body. And now you can receive it back and be able to treat your diabetes.
V/O:
And this is what Joe and his team have managed to achieve – they found a way to take other cells and change them into insulin producing Beta cells. The research took them 10 years.
Joe:
We systematically investigated every cell type and asked the question: Now, which cell in your body can most readily be remade into an insulin secreting Beta cell.
LINK:
Eventually they found the answer and it was quite a surprise.
Joe:
A population of cells that is hiding in your stomach is the cell type.
V/O:
These gastric cells are closely related to Beta cells. They have another advantage – they have a powerful population of stem cells. Stem cells have the ability to quickly proliferate and constantly replenish to regenerate a certain tissue. Skin cells are a good example.
Joe:
Skin has a lot of stem cells because if you scrape your skin the stem cells will proliferate and generate new skin.
V/O:
Stem cells in the stomach also proliferate easily. With a biopsy Joe could harvest a small amount of cells from the stomach. They then grew hundreds of millions of these cells in the lab.

The cells were then structured into individual balls each containing tens of millions of cells. But they were still stomach cells.

To change these cells into Beta cells Joe turned to the human genome. Each cell type has genes that control its identity
Joe:
For example, there are certain genes that tell the liver cells to be liver, and skin cells to be skin and although there are tens of thousands of these genes encoded in our genome, there’s only a very small number of these genes, so called master regulators that control the identity of a specific cell type.
V/O:
They identified 3 genes as Beta cell master regulators.
Joe:
Now if the three of them can work together, they can force the Beta cell identity into a different cell type.
LINK:
Joe and his team were able to switch these three genes on in the millions of cells they grew in their lab. This turned them into insulin secreting Beta cells.
V/O:
The clusters of newly created Beta cells were then transplanted into the liver due to the ample blood supply in this organ.
Joe:
Now the beta cells can talk to the blood vessel and be able to basically monitor the blood sugar level inside the blood and pump out insulin when you need it.
V/O:
And if you have functioning Beta cells in your body, your diabetes is cured.

Joe and his team showed that they could change animal as well as human stomach cells into Beta cells.
Joe:
And we demonstrated that if we do that in the mouse we can now cure the diabetes, if you will, of the mouse by the new beta cells that is made from basically the gastric tissue.
V/O:
Dr Distiller is positive about this new approach.
Distiller:
Yes, I think stem cell research is where it is coming from and where the cure will come from. Whether is it going to be stem cells from another source or from one’s own body they will get there. There is no question about it. Unfortunately it is going to take time.
V/O:
With the huge success in animal studies, the next step is now to move to human trials.
Joe:
Personally I believe this is the best approach to generate a patient specific therapy for beta cell transplantation and replacement to treat diabetes. And we are working very hard to make that happen. I hope it won’t take another ten years.

They confirmed that the mini-organs compensated for the resulting loss of insulin, maintaining glucose at normal levels in five of the 22 experimental animals (this was the team’s expected success rate). What is potentially really great about this approach (once it’s developed for humans) is that a physician will be able to create a patient-specific therapy by simply doing a biopsy (snipping out tissue for analysis) from the patient, grow the cells in the lab (as with the mice), reprogram those cells to produce insulin — and then transplant these cells directly into the patient.** “That’s what we’re working on now,” says Zhou. “We’re very excited.” Research funding was provided by the National Institute of Health, the HSCI, the Timothy Murphy Fund, the Children’s Hospital Boston Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities Research Center, and the Harvard Digestive Diseases Center.
